topics.name: Sigmund Freud
topics.kicker: Founder of psychoanalysis · Mapped the mind’s hidden, unconscious side
topics.briefing: Sigmund Freud believed that dreams, slips of the tongue, and even jokes were secret messages from a hidden part of the mind he called the unconscious. This Austrian doctor spent his career in Vienna listening to patients and built an entirely new way to treat the mind called psychoanalysis. His ideas about the id, the ego, and the superego still shape how people talk about personality today.

topics.kicker: British economist · Said governments should spend to fight recessions
topics.briefing: When the world’s economies collapsed during the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes argued for a bold, controversial fix: have governments spend their way out of trouble. This British economist had already made headlines by predicting that harsh peace terms after World War I would backfire. His 1936 book _The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money_ reshaped how governments fight recessions to this day.

topics.kicker: American cultural anthropologist · Studied growing up across cultures
topics.briefing: At just twenty-three years old, Margaret Mead sailed to the South Pacific island of Samoa to live among teenage girls and study their lives firsthand. Her 1928 book, _Coming of Age in Samoa_, argued that culture, not biology, shapes how difficult or easy growing up can be, and it made her one of the most famous scientists in America. She spent decades doing fieldwork across the Pacific, sometimes alongside her husband and fellow anthropologist Gregory Bateson.

topics.kicker: 1971 psychology study · Stopped early after guards turned abusive
topics.briefing: In the summer of 1971, psychologist Philip Zimbardo turned a Stanford University basement into a fake prison and had college students play “guards” and “prisoners” for what was supposed to be two weeks. topics.briefing: Demand is the economic idea that explains why a brand-new video game costs more on release day than it does a year later: it is simply how much of something people are willing and able to buy at each possible price. Economists graph it as a downward-sloping curve, since people usually want more of something when it gets cheaper and less when it gets pricier. Where that curve crosses the supply curve sets a market’s price.

trap.title: Demand, or quantity demanded?
trap.body: “Demand” is the whole relationship between price and quantity, shown as an entire curve. “Quantity demanded” is just one specific amount at one specific price, a single point sitting on that curve. topics.briefing: Imagine a candy bar that cost a dime in 1950 costing two dollars today — that’s inflation, the steady rise in prices that makes each dollar buy a little less over time. Economists track it every month using the Consumer Price Index, a running list of prices for everyday goods. When it spirals out of control, like in 1920s Germany or Zimbabwe in the 2000s, it is called hyperinflation, and people rush to spend money before it loses even more value.

tossups.p: Milton Friedman argued that growth in the money supply was always and everywhere the true cause of this phenomenon, a core idea of his monetarist school of thought. He once described it as “taxation without legislation,” since no law ever has to pass for it to quietly shrink what people’s money is worth.
tossups.r: The Phillips Curve traditionally plots this phenomenon against unemployment, moving in opposite directions. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices across an economy.

tossups.p: Economist Robert Gordon’s “triangle model” explains this phenomenon through three forces: “demand-pull,” caused by strong consumer demand; “cost-push,” caused by rising production costs; and a “built-in” expectations effect, building on an earlier Keynesian framework. The Mundell-Tobin effect separately links this phenomenon to real interest rates.
tossups.r: It is tracked using the Consumer Price Index, a running measure of a “basket” of everyday goods. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices over time.

tossups.p: During Germany’s Weimar Republic in the 1920s, this phenomenon grew so extreme that people reportedly burned stacks of cash for warmth, since firewood cost more. Decades later, Zimbabwe suffered one of history’s worst bouts of this in the 2000s, eventually printing banknotes worth 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollars.
tossups.r: Modern central banks typically try to keep it at around two percent a year. For 10 points, name this phenomenon of generally rising prices.

tossups.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker sharply raised interest rates around 1980 to beat back a stubborn bout of this phenomenon left over from the 1970s oil crisis. Research by economists Alesina and Summers later found that this phenomenon tends to run lower in countries with more independent central banks.
tossups.r: Businesses that must constantly reprint price tags because of it face so-called “menu costs.” For 10 points, name this general, ongoing rise in prices.

tossups.p: The Tanzi effect suggests that a rising rate of this phenomenon makes it harder for governments to collect taxes effectively, since the real value of overdue payments shrinks. In the Fisher equation, the Greek letter pi represents this phenomenon, linking a loan’s nominal interest rate to its real one.
tossups.r: “Shoe-leather costs” describe the extra trips people make trying to avoid holding on to cash during a bad bout of it. For 10 points, name this phenomenon, a general rise in prices.

tossups.p: “Menu costs” describe what businesses pay to constantly reprint price tags and relabel goods because of this phenomenon, while “shoe-leather costs” describe the extra trips people make trying to avoid holding too much cash. Its “demand-pull” type comes from strong consumer demand outpacing supply, while its “cost-push” type comes from rising production costs.
tossups.r: The Consumer Price Index is the most common way to track it. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices over time.

tossups.p: Economists convert “nominal” dollar figures into “real” ones specifically to strip out the effect of this phenomenon over time. Monetarists sum up its basic cause as “too much money chasing too few goods,” tying it closely to how quickly a country’s money supply grows.
tossups.r: A sister measurement, the Producer Price Index, tracks this same trend before goods ever reach store shelves. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices across an economy.

tossups.p: The Phillips Curve traditionally shows this phenomenon trading off against unemployment, so that pushing one down tends to push the other up. Studies by economists Alesina and Summers found that countries with more independent central banks tend to see lower rates of this phenomenon.
tossups.r: Paul Volcker famously raised interest rates to fight a severe bout of it around 1980. For 10 points, name this general, ongoing rise in prices.

tossups.p: Robert Gordon’s “triangle model” builds on an earlier Keynesian framework to explain this phenomenon through demand-pull, cost-push, and built-in causes working together. Modern central banks typically aim to keep it at around two percent a year rather than eliminate it entirely.
tossups.r: It is most often measured using the Consumer Price Index. For 10 points, name this gradual, ongoing rise in prices.

tossups.p: In the 2000s, prices in Zimbabwe rose so fast that the government eventually issued a banknote worth 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollars to keep up with this phenomenon. A strikingly similar episode struck Germany’s Weimar Republic in the 1920s, when workers reportedly needed wheelbarrows just to carry enough cash for groceries.
tossups.r: The Phillips Curve traditionally plots this phenomenon against the unemployment rate. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices, which can become runaway in extreme cases.

tossups.p: Milton Friedman once likened this phenomenon to a dangerous disease whose only cure is slower growth in the quantity of money. He insisted that it was “always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon,” a central claim of his monetarist school of economics.
tossups.r: The Consumer Price Index tracks it by following the cost of a basket of everyday goods. For 10 points, name this gradual rise in prices that erodes how much a dollar can buy.

tossups.p: The Fisher equation uses the Greek letter pi to represent this phenomenon while relating nominal and real interest rates. The related Mundell-Tobin effect describes a further link between this phenomenon and real interest rates, one whose exact size economists still debate.
tossups.r: Central banks like the Federal Reserve try to slow it down by raising interest rates. For 10 points, name this general rise in prices over time.

tossups.p: “Menu costs” and “shoe-leather costs” are two of the everyday burdens this phenomenon places on businesses and households alike, forcing constant price updates and extra trips to avoid holding cash. Its two best-known types, “demand-pull” and “cost-push,” describe whether strong demand or rising costs is doing the pushing.
tossups.r: Most modern central banks aim to keep it at around two percent a year. For 10 points, name this gradual, ongoing rise in prices across an economy.

tossups.p: The Tanzi effect notes that a surge in this phenomenon can actually hurt a government’s ability to collect taxes in real terms. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker raised interest rates sharply around 1980 to tame a stubborn version of it left over from the 1970s energy crisis.
tossups.r: It is tracked month to month using the Consumer Price Index. For 10 points, name this general, ongoing rise in prices.

tossups.p: Economists Alesina and Summers linked lower rates of this phenomenon to greater independence for a country’s central bank, while Robert Gordon’s triangle model instead explained it through demand-pull, cost-push, and built-in causes working together. Both lines of research tried to explain what drives it.
tossups.r: A unit of currency, like the dollar, buys less and less as this phenomenon continues. For 10 points, name this gradual, ongoing rise in prices.

trap.body: Quiz bowl also asks about “cosmic inflation,” a completely different idea in Astronomy about the universe’s rapid expansion just after the Big Bang. On the economics side, the closest trap is confusing this with deflation, which is the opposite: a FALL in prices, not a rise.

topics.name: Unemployment
topics.kicker: People without jobs who want one · Tracked monthly, tied to the business cycle
topics.briefing: Not everyone without a paycheck counts the same way to economists: unemployment specifically means people who want a job and are actively looking for one but have not found it. The government reports a national rate every month, and economists sort the causes into types, like frictional (between jobs), structural (skills don’t match), and cyclical (tied to recessions). When the rate climbs, it is usually a sign the whole economy is slowing down.

tossups.p: The U.S. government calculates this monthly measurement through the Current Population Survey, conducted door to door and by phone by the Census Bureau. Okun’s Law estimates that a one-point rise in this figure tends to come with roughly a two-percent drop in the nation’s GDP.
tossups.r: The Beveridge Curve plots it against the job vacancy rate, while the Phillips Curve plots it against inflation. For 10 points, name this rate describing the share of people who want work but cannot find it.

tossups.p: Economists split this phenomenon into three main types: “frictional,” the short gap between jobs; “structural,” caused by a mismatch between workers’ skills and available jobs; and “cyclical,” tied to the broader ups and downs of the economy. Adding the frictional and structural types together gives what Milton Friedman called the “natural rate” of this.
tossups.r: It typically rises sharply during recessions and falls during recoveries. For 10 points, identify this measurement of people actively seeking work who have not found any.

tossups.p: People who have given up searching for work entirely are called “discouraged” and are left out of the official count for this measurement, even though they still lack jobs. When the Labor Force Participation Rate falls at the same time as this figure, economists often suspect that discouragement, not new jobs, is the real cause.
tossups.r: Retirees and students are likewise excluded from the count. For 10 points, name this rate of people who are jobless and actively job-hunting.

tossups.p: Replacing human workers with robots and software is a textbook cause of the “structural” type of this phenomenon, since displaced workers often lack the new skills employers need. Keynesian economists also blame “sticky” wages, which fail to fall quickly in a downturn, for worsening this measurement’s “cyclical” type.
tossups.r: A small fourth type, called “seasonal,” comes from jobs like holiday retail work ending on schedule. For 10 points, name this rate of people without jobs who are looking for one.

tossups.p: During the Great Recession, people who had exhausted 99 weeks of benefits and still had not found work earned the nickname “99ers,” a grim symbol of this measurement’s long-term side. A decade later, the 2021 “Great Resignation” did not push this figure up, since many departing workers moved straight to new jobs or retired instead of job-hunting.
tossups.r: It is tracked monthly by the Current Population Survey. For 10 points, name this economic measurement of people without jobs who want one.

tossups.p: The Phillips Curve traditionally shows an inverse relationship between this measurement and inflation, so that pushing one down tends to push the other up. Economist Arthur Okun instead linked it directly to the nation’s output, noting that GDP tends to fall by about two percent for every one-point rise here.
tossups.r: A government survey excludes retired people and full-time students from its count. For 10 points, name this rate describing joblessness among people actively seeking work.

tossups.p: Even in a healthy economy, some of this phenomenon persists as workers take time to search for a better fit, a “frictional” type captured on the Beveridge Curve alongside the job vacancy rate. A mismatch between the skills employers want and the skills workers have instead produces the “structural” version.
tossups.r: This measurement tends to spike sharply whenever a recession hits. For 10 points, name this rate of joblessness among people who want work but cannot find it.

tossups.p: Milton Friedman helped popularize the idea of a “natural rate” for this phenomenon, the level that persists even when the economy is otherwise healthy, made up of its frictional and structural types. This rate rises when automation or outsourcing erases entire categories of jobs.
tossups.r: It is distinct from “underemployment,” which counts people stuck in part-time or lower-skill jobs than they want. For 10 points, name this measurement of joblessness reported as a monthly percentage.

tossups.p: This measurement tends to climb during a recession and fall during an expansion, making it one of the clearest signs of where the business cycle stands. The Labor Force Participation Rate, which tracks how many people are working or looking for work at all, is reported alongside it each month.
tossups.r: Its “cyclical” type disappears once the broader economy recovers. For 10 points, name this rate of people without jobs who are actively seeking one.

tossups.p: A rough rule of thumb known as Okun’s Law holds that each one-percentage-point increase in this figure accompanies about a two-percent loss in a country’s total economic output. The “structural” variety of it often follows waves of automation or offshoring that make older job skills obsolete.
tossups.r: Economists do not count discouraged workers who have stopped searching. For 10 points, name this government-reported rate of joblessness.

tossups.p: The Beveridge Curve compares this rate to the number of open job postings, called the vacancy rate, across the economy. A short-term version called “frictional” simply reflects the ordinary time it takes someone to find a new position after leaving an old one.
tossups.r: This rate rose sharply during the Great Recession of 2008 and 2009. For 10 points, name this measurement of the percentage of people without jobs who are looking for one.

tossups.p: Keynesian economists argue that wages which are “sticky downward,” meaning they resist falling even during a slump, help explain why this phenomenon’s cyclical type can linger after a recession technically ends. Its structural type, by contrast, can persist for years as entire industries shrink or relocate.
tossups.r: Retirees, by definition, are not included when the government calculates this rate. For 10 points, name this measurement of joblessness among people actively job-hunting.

tossups.p: A nationwide survey conducted monthly by the Census Bureau asks adults whether they currently have a job and, if not, whether they are actively searching for one, in order to calculate this figure. The “natural rate” version of it combines the frictional and structural types and persists even in a booming economy.
tossups.r: This rate and inflation are shown moving in opposite directions on the Phillips Curve. For 10 points, name this percentage of the labor force without jobs.

tossups.p: When both this measurement and the Labor Force Participation Rate fall in the same month, economists often suspect that discouraged workers have simply stopped looking rather than that the job market has truly improved. Replacing workers with machines is a leading cause of its longer-lasting “structural” form.
tossups.r: It rises during recessions and falls during recoveries, tracking the business cycle closely. For 10 points, name this rate of people out of work who want a job.

tossups.p: Despite millions of workers quitting their jobs during the 2021 “Great Resignation,” this measurement did not rise, since many quitters moved straight to new jobs or retired instead of job-hunting. A smaller “seasonal” type rises and falls predictably, for instance when holiday retail jobs end each January.
tossups.r: Economists sort most of it into frictional, structural, and cyclical types. For 10 points, name this rate describing people without jobs who are actively looking for one.

trap.body: Some real tossups use this concept only as a clue inside a tossup whose actual answer is “labor” or “the labor force” — one real set defines the rate as the share of people NOT doing a certain activity, and that activity, not this rate, is the intended answer. topics.name: Anthropology
topics.kicker: The study of human cultures and societies · From fieldwork to ancient artifacts
topics.dates: Became a university discipline in the late 1800s
topics.briefing: What do a stone tool, a word’s grammar, a skeleton, and a wedding ceremony have in common? They are all evidence anthropologists use to understand what makes people people. This “study of humankind” splits into subfields covering culture, the human body, ancient remains, and language, and pioneers like Franz Boas and his students helped turn it into a rigorous university discipline in the early 1900s.

tossups.p: Before becoming a professor, one founding figure in this field studied the migrations of Inuit communities on Canada’s Baffin Island in the 1880s. That researcher, Franz Boas, later developed the idea of “cultural relativism,” judging a culture by its own standards instead of outside ones, while training generations of students at Columbia University.
tossups.r: His book _The Mind of Primitive Man_ challenged racist theories of his day. For 10 points, name this social science that studies human cultures and societies.

tossups.p: One researcher in this field spent months on the Pacific island of Samoa interviewing teenage girls for her landmark 1928 book, _Coming of Age in Samoa_. That researcher, Margaret Mead, studied under Franz Boas at Columbia alongside classmates who became leaders in the same discipline.
tossups.r: Practitioners of this field often live for months inside the community they are studying, a method called fieldwork. For 10 points, name this field devoted to the study of human cultures.

tossups.p: Researcher Ruth Benedict studied Japanese culture “at a distance” during World War II, partly through interviews conducted in Japanese internment camps in the United States, since she could not travel there herself. Her resulting book, _The Chrysanthemum and the Sword_, contrasted Japan’s “shame culture” with what she called the West’s “guilt culture.”
tossups.r: Benedict had earlier argued that every culture has its own consistent personality in _Patterns of Culture_. For 10 points, name this discipline that studies human societies and their customs.

tossups.p: Bronislaw Malinowski [“broh-NEE-swahf mah-lih-NOF-skee”] pioneered “participant observation” in this field by living for years among the Trobriand Islanders of Melanesia instead of simply reading other travelers’ reports. His 1922 book, _Argonauts of the Western Pacific_, described the Kula ring, a ceremonial exchange of shell jewelry between neighboring islands.
tossups.r: Researchers in this field who focus on living cultures often call their detailed written studies ethnographies. For 10 points, name this field, the study of human societies and cultures.

tossups.p: Before she became a celebrated novelist, one figure connected to this field trained under Franz Boas at Columbia and Barnard and collected folklore across the American South, Haiti, and Jamaica. That researcher and writer, Zora Neale Hurston, applied her training in this discipline to her fiction.
tossups.r: This discipline’s name comes from Greek words meaning the “study of humankind.” For 10 points, name this field, which examines human cultures, biology, language, and the past.

tossups.p: This discipline is often divided into four main subfields: cultural, which studies living societies; biological, which studies human evolution and variation; archaeological, which studies physical remains of past peoples; and linguistic, which studies language in its cultural setting. Researchers in its cultural branch often spend months doing fieldwork within a single community.
tossups.r: Franz Boas trained many of the field’s early American pioneers at Columbia University. For 10 points, name this field, the broad study of human societies and cultures.

tossups.p: A detailed written account of a culture, built from months of fieldwork, is called an ethnography in this discipline. Early practitioners of this field sometimes relied only on other travelers’ secondhand reports until Bronislaw Malinowski’s firsthand stay among the Trobriand Islanders helped make direct fieldwork the standard.
tossups.r: This field is often compared with sociology, though it traditionally takes a broader, more cross-cultural view. For 10 points, name this field devoted to studying human cultures and societies.

tossups.p: Margaret Mead’s 1928 study of adolescence among girls on Samoa became one of the most widely read books ever written in this field, though later researchers questioned some of her conclusions. Mead studied at Columbia under Franz Boas, the same mentor who trained Ruth Benedict and Zora Neale Hurston.
tossups.r: This discipline’s name derives from Greek roots meaning “the study of humankind.” For 10 points, name this field that studies human cultures, past and present.

tossups.p: Ruth Benedict’s _The Chrysanthemum and the Sword_ popularized the influential, if later debated, distinction between “guilt cultures” and “shame cultures.” Her mentor, Franz Boas, had earlier used this discipline to argue against so-called “scientific racism” in his book _The Mind of Primitive Man_.
tossups.r: The field’s biological subfield instead studies human evolution and variation across populations. For 10 points, name this discipline, the broad study of human societies and cultures.

tossups.p: Before becoming a professor, one founder of modern fieldwork methods in this discipline studied Inuit migration on Baffin Island; another, Bronislaw Malinowski, developed “participant observation” while living among Pacific islanders he described in _Argonauts of the Western Pacific_. Both approaches replaced older reliance on secondhand travelers’ accounts.
tossups.r: This discipline includes cultural, biological, archaeological, and linguistic subfields. For 10 points, name this field, the broad study of humankind.

tossups.p: This field’s archaeological subfield examines tools, pottery, and other physical remains left behind by past peoples, while its linguistic subfield studies how language reflects and shapes culture. Its biological subfield traces human evolution and the variation found across living populations today.
tossups.r: Its cultural subfield relies heavily on fieldwork, living inside a community to study it firsthand. For 10 points, name this broad field, the study of human societies past and present.

tossups.p: Zora Neale Hurston once described her Columbia training in this discipline as giving her an outsider’s lens for looking at her own community in the American South. Her teacher, Franz Boas, had spent his own early career documenting Inuit life on Baffin Island before developing the idea of cultural relativism.
tossups.r: Ruth Benedict and Margaret Mead were two of Boas’s other famous students in this field. For 10 points, name this discipline that studies human cultures and societies.

tossups.p: This discipline takes its name from Greek words meaning “the study of humankind,” and it is often compared with sociology, though it traditionally takes a broader, more cross-cultural view of human life. Bronislaw Malinowski helped establish fieldwork, living among the people being studied, as this field’s defining method.
tossups.r: Franz Boas and his students, including Margaret Mead and Ruth Benedict, shaped the field’s early years in the United States. For 10 points, name this field, the study of human cultures.

tossups.p: In _Patterns of Culture_, researcher Ruth Benedict argued that every society has its own consistent cultural “personality.” This field’s archaeological subfield, meanwhile, pieces together the lives of long-vanished peoples using tools, pottery, and other physical remains they left behind.
tossups.r: Its name comes from Greek words meaning the study of humankind. For 10 points, identify this broad field devoted to studying human societies and cultures.

tossups.p: Bronislaw Malinowski’s years living among the Trobriand Islanders, studying the ceremonial Kula ring, helped define the fieldwork methods still used in this discipline today. Columbia University, meanwhile, became an early American hub for the field under Franz Boas, who trained Margaret Mead, Ruth Benedict, and Zora Neale Hurston.
tossups.r: This discipline’s linguistic subfield studies how language shapes and reflects culture. For 10 points, name this field, the study of human societies and cultures.

trap.title: Names are not the field
trap.body: These tossups are packed with names: Franz Boas, Ruth Benedict, Margaret Mead, Bronislaw Malinowski, Zora Neale Hurston. They are all famous people IN this field, not the answer. Quiz bowl also has separate tossups just on Margaret Mead herself, so naming her here is a different, and wrong, answer line. Two related fields come up too: sociology, which leans toward modern societies, and archaeology, which is just one piece of this broader field.
trap.fix: Wait for the describing word: “this discipline,” “this field,” or “this social science” means the whole subject, even right after a famous researcher’s name is read. Only buzz with a person’s name if the clue asks to name that person.

topics.kicker: A market with just one seller · Countered by antitrust law since 1890
topics.briefing: Picture a town with only one power company and no other choice for electricity — that town is stuck dealing with a monopoly, a market with just one seller and no real competition. Without rivals pushing prices down, that seller can charge more and decide how much to produce. High barriers that keep new competitors out, like huge startup costs, help monopolies survive, which is why the United States has passed antitrust laws since 1890 to break them up or keep them in check.

tossups.p: The Coase Conjecture [“kohs”] holds that a seller of a long-lasting good in this market structure must start by pricing low, since it will eventually compete against its own already-sold units. Profit here is still maximized where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, but the seller then charges whatever higher price the demand curve allows at that output.
tossups.r: High barriers to entry, like huge startup costs, keep rivals from challenging a seller in this position. For 10 points, name this market structure in which a single seller faces no real competition.

tossups.p: The Lerner Index, built from the gap between price and marginal cost, measures how much pricing power a seller holds in this market structure, with values closer to one signaling greater power. Because output here falls below the competitive quantity, this situation also creates what economists call deadweight loss.
tossups.r: The United States has passed antitrust laws since 1890 to break up or regulate firms in this position. For 10 points, name this market structure with only one seller.

tossups.p: Economies of scale often create a “natural” version of this market structure, making it cheapest for just one company to serve an entire market, as with water or electric utilities. The Ramsey problem asks how a regulated firm stuck in exactly this position should set prices that still cover its costs.
tossups.r: A single seller here can set a higher price than it could if it faced competition. For 10 points, name this market structure in which one seller controls an entire market.

tossups.p: In 1911, the Supreme Court used American antitrust law to break up Standard Oil, one of history’s most famous examples of this market structure. Nineteenth-century business combinations called “trusts” gave antitrust law its very name, since they often created exactly this kind of single-seller control over an industry.
tossups.r: High barriers to entry typically protect a seller in this position from new rivals. For 10 points, name this market structure defined by a single seller and no real competition.

tossups.p: Because it faces no close competitors, a seller in this market structure can sometimes charge different customers different prices for an identical good, a practice called price discrimination. Patents and copyrights can create temporary, government-granted versions of this situation by giving one company sole rights to sell something for a set number of years.
tossups.r: Profit is maximized here where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. For 10 points, name this market structure in which only one seller exists.

tossups.p: This market structure differs from “monopolistic competition,” where many sellers offer similar but not identical products, and from an oligopoly, where just a few large sellers compete. It is also distinct from a monopsony, the mirror-image situation with only one buyer instead of one seller.
tossups.r: A natural version of this market structure often arises in utilities like electricity and water, thanks to economies of scale. For 10 points, name this market structure with a single seller.

tossups.p: Unlike a firm in a competitive market, a seller in this position is called a “price maker” rather than a “price taker,” since it can set its own price instead of accepting one set by the market. High barriers to entry, whether natural economies of scale or legal protections like patents, keep this position from being challenged.
tossups.r: Antitrust laws exist partly to counter sellers in this position. For 10 points, name this market structure in which a single seller dominates an entire industry.

tossups.p: The Ramsey problem addresses how a regulated seller in this market structure, often a utility, should price its product to best serve the public while still covering its costs. The Coase Conjecture, by contrast, points out that a seller of a durable good in this position loses pricing power over time as it competes with its own past sales.
tossups.r: A single seller with no close competitors defines this market structure. For 10 points, name this situation faced by just one seller of a good or service.

tossups.p: Because output in this market structure sits below the level that would exist under full competition, economists say it creates deadweight loss, a measure of lost economic efficiency. Like any profit-maximizing firm, though, a seller here still produces at the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
tossups.r: Huge barriers to entry typically protect a seller’s position here from new competitors. For 10 points, name this market structure with just one seller.

tossups.p: The nineteenth-century business combinations called “trusts” lent their name to the antitrust laws that now exist to fight this market structure. Standard Oil was perhaps the most famous target of those laws before its breakup by the Supreme Court in 1911.
tossups.r: A single company with no real rivals defines this type of market. For 10 points, name this market structure with only one seller.

tossups.p: A patent can grant an inventor a temporary, legal version of this market structure by giving one company exclusive rights to sell an invention for a set number of years. Because it faces no close rivals, a seller in this position can sometimes charge different prices to different customers for the very same product.
tossups.r: Economies of scale can also create a “natural” version of this situation, especially among utilities. For 10 points, name this market structure defined by a single seller.

tossups.p: A monopsony is sometimes described as the mirror image of this market structure, since it involves only one buyer instead of one seller. An oligopoly, meanwhile, differs from this market structure by having a few large sellers instead of just one.
tossups.r: High barriers to entry keep new sellers from breaking into a market controlled by this structure. For 10 points, identify this market structure in which a single seller faces no competition.

tossups.p: A seller in this position sets its price above marginal cost, unlike a competitive firm, because it faces no rivals pushing prices back down toward cost. Profit is still maximized at the output level where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, even though the price charged ends up higher than that cost.
tossups.r: Governments regulate or break up firms in this position using antitrust law. For 10 points, name this market structure featuring one seller and no real competition.

tossups.p: Water, electricity, and other utilities are classic real-world examples of a “natural” version of this market structure, since economies of scale make a single large provider more efficient than several competing ones. Economists studying the Ramsey problem have asked how such a regulated seller should set prices that still cover its costs.
tossups.r: Antitrust laws exist to break up or restrain sellers that hold this kind of market power. For 10 points, name this market structure with a single seller and high barriers to entry.

tossups.p: Before its 1911 breakup, Standard Oil controlled most of the American oil industry, becoming a textbook historical example of this market structure in action. High barriers to entry, like enormous startup costs or exclusive legal rights, typically protect a seller’s hold on this kind of position.
tossups.r: A single seller with no close competitors defines this type of market structure, which antitrust law exists to counter. For 10 points, name this market structure with just one seller.

trap.title: Board game and look-alike terms
trap.body: Quiz bowl sometimes asks trivia or pop-culture questions about the Monopoly board game (Parker Brothers, Boardwalk, the “Go to Jail” space) — that is a completely different kind of question from this economics term, even though the word is spelled the same. Inside economics, this term also has close cousins that are NOT the same: monopolistic competition (many sellers, slightly different products) and monopsony (one BUYER instead of one seller).
trap.fix: Clues about dice, tokens, properties, or rent mean the board game. Clues about market structure, a single seller, barriers to entry, or antitrust law mean this economic concept. If the clue says “many sellers” or “one buyer,” that is a different market structure — do not buzz with this answer.
